**Ed McMahon, the booming-voiced “second banana” who helped make late-night television feel like America’s living room, dies at 86**

Ed McMahon, the durable entertainer whose signature “Heeeere’s Johnny!” became one of television’s most recognizable calls to attention, died June 23, 2009, at age 86. Though he worked as a broadcaster, pitchman, game-show host, talent-show presenter and commercial spokesman, McMahon’s place in television history rests most securely on the 30 years he spent beside Johnny Carson on NBC’s *The Tonight Show*.

McMahon was often called the ultimate “second banana” — an old show-business phrase for the comic partner who is not the star but is essential to the act. In vaudeville and early radio comedy, the “top banana” got the big laughs and the spotlight; the “second banana” set up jokes, reacted, took pratfalls, absorbed insults and kept the rhythm moving. It was a support role, but not a minor one. A great second banana could make the headliner look effortless.

McMahon did exactly that.

From 1962 until Carson’s farewell in 1992, McMahon occupied the chair to Carson’s right, laughing loudly, leaning in at just the right moment, and offering the host a dependable target, foil and emotional anchor. He introduced Carson each night with theatrical gusto, but once the monologue began, McMahon’s real job was subtler: he listened. He laughed when the audience needed permission to laugh. He groaned when a joke bombed. He bantered when Carson wanted company and backed away when the host wanted silence. He could take a teasing remark about his drinking, his weight, his commercials or his genial square-jawed image and turn it into warmth rather than embarrassment.

That was the genius of the role. McMahon never competed with Carson. He amplified him.

On *The Tonight Show*, the host’s desk became a kind of American hearth, and McMahon helped define the architecture of late-night television that still exists today: the bandleader, the announcer, the monologue, the guest couch, and the sidekick as both comic partner and audience surrogate. Later late-night figures — from Andy Richter beside Conan O’Brien to announcer-sidekicks on various talk shows — inherited a template McMahon helped perfect. The sidekick could be a friend, a foil, a laugh track, a safety net and a symbol of continuity all at once.

McMahon’s booming introduction was only the most obvious part of his contribution. His presence told viewers that the show was beginning, that the mood was safe, and that Carson — sometimes sly, sometimes aloof, sometimes cutting — had beside him a big-hearted companion who could soften the edges. Carson’s wit could be dry and dangerous; McMahon’s laugh made it communal.

People who worked in late-night television remembered him that way: as a professional who understood the delicate mechanics of making another performer shine. Band members and staffers from the Carson era often described McMahon as unfailingly prepared, affable and generous backstage. He had the bearing of a Marine — he served as a fighter pilot in World War II and was recalled during the Korean War — but the instincts of an old-school entertainer who knew that timing, deference and reliability were everything.

Doc Severinsen, the flamboyant trumpeter and bandleader of *The Tonight Show*, long spoke of McMahon as an indispensable part of the program’s chemistry. In the Carson format, Severinsen’s band provided the energy, Carson provided the wit, and McMahon provided the connective tissue — the booming welcome, the rolling laugh, the sense that a joke had landed even before the studio audience fully reacted. Tommy Newsom, the band’s famously deadpan substitute leader, was also part of that comic ecosystem: Carson would needle Newsom, McMahon would laugh, Severinsen would play, and the show’s family dynamic would reassert itself.

Jay Leno, who inherited *The Tonight Show* after Carson retired, remembered McMahon as a foundational figure in the franchise — not merely Carson’s announcer, but part of the reason the show’s rituals mattered. David Letterman, whose own late-night career was deeply shaped by Carson’s example, often treated the Carson-McMahon era as the gold standard: elegant, controlled, adult and deceptively difficult to imitate. For later generations of hosts, McMahon represented a kind of craftsmanship that could be easy to overlook because it looked so natural.

McMahon’s partnership with Carson began before *The Tonight Show*, on the daytime game show *Who Do You Trust?* in the late 1950s. There they developed the rapport that would later become central to late night: Carson as the quick, ironic, sometimes mischievous host; McMahon as the hearty announcer and companion who could keep the exchange grounded. When Carson took over *Tonight* from Jack Paar in 1962, McMahon came with him, and the pairing became one of television’s longest and most successful marriages of personalities.

The two were not the same man. Carson was famously private and complex, more comfortable behind the desk than in public intimacy. McMahon was gregarious, expansive and seemingly born to work a room. That contrast helped the show. Carson could retreat into cool wit because McMahon radiated warmth. McMahon could be broad because Carson was precise. Together, they created a rhythm that felt spontaneous even when it rested on decades of practice.

Beyond late night, McMahon became a familiar face in other corners of American popular culture. He hosted *Star Search*, the nationally syndicated talent competition that helped introduce performers including future stars of music, comedy and television. He appeared in commercials, variety specials, blooper programs and telethons. He was also widely recognized for his work with the American Family Publishers sweepstakes, showing up at doors — or seeming to — as the bearer of giant checks. In later years, financial and health troubles brought unwelcome tabloid attention, including reports that he faced foreclosure on his Beverly Hills home. But those difficulties did little to dim the affection many viewers felt for him.

His death prompted not only nostalgia for a performer but reflection on an era of television that had largely vanished. Carson’s *Tonight Show* was a national ritual in a way few programs can be now, airing before a fragmented media landscape split audiences into countless niches. McMahon’s voice was part of that ritual. For millions, “Heeeere’s Johnny!” meant the day was ending with wit, polish and company.

The phrase “second banana” can sound diminutive, as if the performer in that role is merely secondary. McMahon’s career proved the opposite. In comedy, being second requires discipline. It requires ego control, timing and emotional intelligence. It requires knowing when to speak, when to laugh, when to be the butt of the joke and when to disappear completely. McMahon made those skills visible by making them seem invisible.

He did not simply sit next to Johnny Carson. He helped create the conditions in which Carson could be Johnny Carson.

That is why Ed McMahon’s legacy is larger than a catchphrase. He defined what a television sidekick could be: loyal but not bland, funny but not disruptive, familiar but never bigger than the show. He was the laugh beside the desk, the voice before the curtain rose, the companion who made late night feel less like a performance and more like a visit.

And for three decades, when Ed McMahon told America that Johnny was here, America believed the night could begin.
